nameStory: The delightful name "plums-and-custard" perfectly captures this mushroom's striking color scheme. The cap displays rich purplish-red tones reminiscent of ripe plums, while the gills beneath are a creamy yellow-white like thick custard. It's one of those wonderfully descriptive common names that makes identification almost as easy as ordering dessert!
description: Plums-and-custard is a medium-sized gilled mushroom that looks like someone mixed fruit and dessert colors on a forest floor. The cap ranges from 2-4 inches across and features beautiful reddish-purple to wine-colored tones, often with a slightly fuzzy or scaly texture. Beneath the colorful cap, creamy yellow-white gills create a striking contrast, while the stem echoes the cap's reddish hues. This eye-catching fungus grows on decaying coniferous wood, making it a delightful discovery during woodland walks.

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Rich reddish-purple to wine-colored, 2-4 inches across, often with small scales or a slightly velvety texture that feels soft to the touch

idTips.label: Gills
idTips.description: Creamy yellow to pale yellow-white, creating a beautiful contrast with the dark cap; gills are attached to the stem and fairly crowded together

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Usually reddish-brown with darker reddish scales or fibers, especially toward the base; feels firm and fibrous when gently squeezed

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: Pleasant, mild mushroomy odor without any strong or unpleasant notes; some describe it as slightly fruity or earthy

idTips.label: Spore Print
idTips.description: White to pale cream colored when spores are collected on paper; helps distinguish from similar-looking species

habitat: Look for plums-and-custard growing on dead or dying coniferous wood throughout New England's forests, particularly on pine, spruce, and fir logs and stumps. They prefer moist woodland environments and are often found in mixed coniferous-deciduous forests at various elevations. You'll typically spot them growing in small groups or clusters rather than alone.

seasonality.spring: Early fruiting may begin in late spring during warm, wet periods, especially on well-rotted conifer logs that have retained moisture.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for plums-and-custard, particularly after summer rains when humidity is high and temperatures are warm but not extreme.
seasonality.fall: Continues fruiting well into autumn, often producing some of the most vibrant specimens as cooler, damper conditions return to the forest.
seasonality.winter: Rarely fruits in winter, though dried specimens from earlier seasons may persist on logs as papery remnants.

funFact: Despite its dessert-like name and appetizing appearance, plums-and-custard mushrooms actually help recycle forest nutrients by breaking down tough conifer wood with specialized enzymes that can dissolve lignin - the same compound that makes wood hard enough for construction!
confusionNotes: The distinctive plum-and-custard color combination makes this species fairly unique, but beginners might confuse it with other reddish mushrooms growing on wood. Remember the key combo: reddish-purple cap PLUS yellow gills PLUS conifer wood - most other red mushrooms lack this specific three-part combination.
contextualKnowledge: This mushroom is sometimes called "red-haired agaric" in older field guides, referring to the reddish, hair-like scales on the cap and stem. The scientific name "rutilans" means "glowing red," highlighting how the reddish colors can seem to glow against the dark forest floor.
compareHints: Plums-and-custard stands out among its Tricholomopsis relatives primarily due to its distinctive reddish-purple coloration and preference for coniferous wood. The related Decorated Mop has more yellow tones overall and lacks the rich plum colors, while other species in the genus tend to be more uniformly colored rather than showing the dramatic plum-and-custard contrast. The combination of reddish cap, yellow gills, and conifer substrate makes this the most easily identified member of its genus.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Tricholomopsis relatives, Decorated Mop stands out with its distinctive purple-brown and yellow color pattern.
